speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to support the motion moved by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). Members of this Party can agree with nearly everything he said.
For many years now Liberal and Conservative Governments have recognized, as have the Governments of most if not all modern industrialized countries, that artists, whether they be visual artists, musicians or artists of other types, need support if they are to create the works they want to create. Very few artists are in a position to support themselves through the sale of their work.
Over the years, regardless of which Party forms the Government, we have given support to artists and performers of various types through the Canada Council, through the CBC, through grants from the Department of the Secretary of State and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. But recently, Revenue Canada has come forward with an aggressive policy of zeroing in on artists, musicians and writers in an attempt to reclassify them and make them pay income tax on income three or four years back.
A month ago I put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) and requested him to put a stop to the present policy of the Department until the matter could be reassessed and re-examined as is suggested in the motion of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead. At the same time, questions were put to the Minister by Members of the Official Opposition and a Liberal Member asked a question about the Toronto Symphony. All Members got a pretty negative or pretty hostile reply.
There are not many Tony Onleys in Canada who have $1 million worth of art to sell. Most artists in this country are poor. Most artists in this country are living in poverty. The Applebaum-Hebert Committee, for example, found that only one of every five Canadian artists earns a gross income of over $5,000, that 60 per cent of artists in a sample survey conducted in Ontario were living in desperate conditions, and that the most recent estimates show that 80 per cent of visual artists in Canada earn less than $7,250 in direct art sales every year.
Recently, Revenue Canada suddenly made a ruling that members of the Toronto Symphony Orchestra are to be classified as employees. That will mean that they will not be able to deduct their expenses as musicians for tax purposes. Members of the Toronto Symphony have a contract which says that they are guaranteed 48 weeks of work per year but only 19.5 hours per week. It is pretty obvious to anyone, except to officials of Revenue Canada, that musicians must have other employment as they cannot live on what they earn with the orchestra. It is important to them that they be able to deduct their expenses as musicians from income as musicians. Yet Revenue Canada has told them that they cannot do that.
November 2, 1983

Now Revenue Canada is going after writers. Very few writers in Canada can earn a living just by writing. Like many other artists, some of them try to teach, if not every year, perhaps one year in two or one in three or four. That way they can at least have an income they can count on for one year. Now Revenue Canada is starting to put the squeeze on them.
The Minister has been saying that Revenue Canada is only interpreting the law. I find it strange that in 1983 Revenue Canada is making interpretations it never made before. Not only is it being unreasonable about the current year or the last year, but it is going back three and four years and expecting artists, musicians and 1 suppose writers to account for everything they have done. That is really impossible.
Like the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead, I have had representations from artists and musicians from Vancouver to Halifax. Some of the cases are beyond belief. In Montreal a well known sculptor received a letter from Revenue Canada telling him that it had arbitrarily-and that is the Department's term-decided that his claim for art materials, supplies and expenses is not admissible and that he must pay $8,000 within the next three months. Apparently grants which he has received from the Canada Council to go toward his expenses were judged to represent the extent of his costs. Other costs were disallowed.
In Vancouver an artist was given 21 days to prove that his activities as an artist showed a reasonable expectation of profit. He wants to know how one can prove to Revenue Canada that a reasonable expectation of profit exists in the research, development production, promotion and sale of original works of art.
1 would ask Hon. Members to think about some of the most famous artists in the world-Picasso, Gaugin, Van Gogh or any other. When those artists produced their works they could barely give them away, but those works are now worth millions of dollars. Revenue Canada is asking our artists to classify themselves as manufacturers. How does an artist know that the work he produced in 1982 or 1983 will sell or for how much it will sell? The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead blamed the computer. I blame the people who stopped using their heads and substituted the computer.
Another artist who was the recipient of an honour from the Governor General which made him a Royal Canadian artist is now subject to niggling scrutiny by Revenue Canada for every cent he spends on art supplies. He said that the action by Revenue Canada makes him feel that the honour he received is ludicrous.
All these cases bring us back to one glaring reality: the Government, as represented by Revenue Canada in its efforts to maximize revenue, has lost all perspective of the role of arts and culture in the life of this country. The attack on Canadian visual and performing artists has the potential of retarding the development of arts in this country.
If the present policy of Revenue Canada continues, artists will stop producing. They are already living in poverty and will not be able to afford to continue working. This attacks the
Income Tax Act
most vulnerable group in society. At the same time we have a tax department which permits people who make large amounts of money to pay little or no tax on huge incomes.
Jack McArthur, who regularly writes a business column in the Toronto Star pointed out some of the things which go on in this country. He pointed out that in 1980 there were 179 people in Canada with incomes of more than $200,000 who did not pay any income tax at all; that there were 651 Canadians who had incomes of between $100,000 and $200,000 who did not pay any income tax; that there were 4,020 who had incomes of between $50,000 and $100,000 who did not pay any income tax.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Revenue and his Department would be doing a much better job in thinking more realistically and more humanely about the burden of taxation which we all have to face if they would concentrate their efforts in trying to plug the loopholes which permit a relatively small number of very large income earners to pay no income tax at all. They should not be concentrating on artists, musicians and writers whose incomes are quite small and who need assistance, help and sympathy from the Canadian Government, rather than the kind of harassment they have received in the last few years.
I have raised this question during the question period and I have arranged, as well as other Hon. Members, I am sure, for meetings between the representatives of the artists and musicians and representatives of the Canadian Conference on the Arts, when I could not reach the Minister. They had a very good discussion and afterward both sides understood better what the other side was talking about. It was obvious that the Assistant Deputy Minister either could not or would not budge. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is time for the Government to act. I believe the idea of a parliamentary committee to look at this question is a good one.
I wish that we could look more seriously and more quickly at the recommendations made in the Disney Report. I say to the Minister of National Revenue that until this committee meets, has an opportunity to hear representations and makes its report, and until the Government can act on the report, the Minister ought to say to his people in Revenue Canada: "Stop this harassment. Stop this drive to collect what will actually be very small amounts of money." Let us go back to the period of a year ago when the Department was looking at these things with a relatively humane attitude. Until then, Mr. Speaker, we certainly support the concept of establishing this committee.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: TAXATION OF VISUAL AND PERFORMING ARTISTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) for introducing this topic and bringing it forward for discussion today. 1 agree with the motion. I would like to offer some amendments which I believe would help us to operate more easily with the idea. Hopefully, it will expedite our treatment of the idea. I would like to come back to the amendments in a few minutes. However, let me

November 2, 1983
Income Tax Act
congratulate the Right Hon. Member for bringing this topic forward.
I come from a background in book publishing. For some 12 years before I was elected I had some experience as an editor and salesman in the book industry. Therefore, 1 feel I understand something about the problems facing writers in just generating income, let alone getting as far as paying their taxes. Many writers, as has been eloquently stated here, are really very underpaid. We do not in any way reflect in our financial rewards any gratitude at all for the heritage which they are leaving for our country's future, and the great enrichment of our country to which writers are contributing. I know the same is true for visual artists and for performing artists, as the Right Hon. Member noted earlier.
I would like as well to draw attention to the key document, the Applebaum-Hebert Report, the recent survey of the arts in Canada. This study has had a significant impact already and has been referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. That Committee has been reviewing portions of the study. It has completed one significant part, I believe on broadcasting, and is now turning its attention to artists, writers and the performing arts. Therefore, this motion presented by the Right Hon. Member fits in in a very timely way with the study of the Committee on Communications and Culture.
Before I continue, 1 would like to draw to everyone's attention what I consider to be a refreshing move by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres). Earlier this week something happened in response to a query by the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) and earlier from the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) and, 1 believe, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). Those Hon. Members have been inquiring about the audit by Revenue Canada of the Toronto Symphony Orchestra. The Minister, because he wanted to be fair, ordered a moratorium on the ruling. He has subsequently met with members of the orchestra. The meeting was very fruitful. I attended the meeting and I feel that the ruling will be reviewed carefully in light of the discussions at that meeting. Certainly, the musicians and their representatives are getting a full day in court from a very sensitive and practical Minister.
I referred a moment ago to the work of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture which is working with the Applebaum-Hebert Report. I will have some amendments to this motion to send to that Committee to tie it into the study of the Applebaum-Hebert Report. That Committee has the expertise to appreciate the story from the artists' perspective rather than from a financial perspective. Therefore, it is appropriate that a motion like this should go to such a group. The artistic community will get its best hearing from that Committee. Certainly, they would be talking to people who understand their working conditions, living standards and the tax problem these people face. The best audience for a motion like this is in the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
I know that the Hon. Member for London West (Mr. Burghardt), who is a Parliamentary Secretary working on that Committee, would like to say a few things in a moment about the work of the Committee.
The Applebaum-Hebert Report made several comments on its insight into the nature of these tax problems. It listed several tax problems as follows, if I may quote from that report:
-matters such as the treatment of artists' costs (and whether or in what circumstances artists should be considered as employees or self-employed), the valuation of works donated by artists to public institutions, and the incomeaveraging tax provisions available... Although such proposals may appear to the department of Finance to require departures from standard practices, to the extent that they involve nothing more than simple equity they can scarcely be construed as special pleading-
That line of thought coincides quite closely with the presentation of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead. The issue over the past few years really has been that artists have been treated as if they are business people or businesses per se. Of course, there is no need to do that. However, that parallel has come about because we have been trying to treat all taxpayers equally.
The question of tax equity has arisen. If we depart from that standard, we must do so carefully because potentially we will be favouring one group and at the same time creating an incentive for a lot of other people to call themselves members of that special group. Before we depart from that standard, we must ensure that we can define who is the artist and why they are getting special treatment. In general I invite the Committee to turn its mind to that particular problem.
Let me take a few examples and just ask for the Committee's advice. The Right Hon. Member raised the question of what is known as the accrual method of accounting. To state it simply, you cannot write off or deduct an expense until the item for which the expense was incurred has either been sold or declared unsaleable. That system applies for all businesses. According to the description of the Right Hon. Member, it is that system which caused Mr. Tony Onley so much trouble. Of course, an artist would like to use the cash system, as would a lot of small businesses. One can write off the expense in the same year it is incurred and you do not have to wait until the item is sold or declared unsaleable. We use the cash system with farmers. But in a debate about farmers we find in a very revealing way the problems you incur with the cash system for one group and the accrual system for another.
Many people would love to have access to the cash system. In my neighbourhood, for example, in Mississauga, there are not a lot of farmers. There is a lot of vacant land and a lot of people sitting on that land and they would love to be able to call themselves farmers and take advantage of the cash system. It would give them a better write-off and they would be able to mix in a lot of different things under this disguise of being a farmer. So I think when the Committee goes to work on this problem it should indeed take a look at potential abuses in the cash system. It looks so temptingly easy and yet farmers'
November 2, 1983

representatives, such as the Cattlemen's Association, said to me last spring they do not want to lose the cash system and they do not want to have the Government loosen up its regulations and invite abuses of the cash system. Equally, if artists want to have this marvellous advantage, let us hope the Committee will give us some definitions of what an artist is, as well as the areas of potential abuse. Artists can do that. They would have no problem telling us how to define themselves. So we invite artists to come in and then perhaps a committee can look at ways to turn their definitions into a workable taxable definitions.
In the same way let us take a look at another problem. The tax department says to businesses that they have to operate with a reasonable expectation of profit. You cannot set up a business just to write off your living expenses. I know some people like to do that. A lovely yacht, a trip here or there, and people would love to have those kinds of write-offs. It would be a terrific incentive. But the tax department will not let you do that. You cannot write off simple living expenses.
One way to define the difference between legitimate business expenses or personal expenses is to ask whether the person has a reasonable expectation of profit. That is how they do it with a business. That is a reasonable standard. But how do you do it with an artist? How do you do it with someone, for example, who has a brilliant ability but simply has not sold anything, such as a young artist just launching his or her career? Obviously such a person will not have a reasonable expectation of profit in the first few years of his or her career.
I must say there is a butcher near my house who claims that in his early years Danby offered him a print in return for some pork chops. Certainly the print appreciated in value a lot faster than those pork chops and it would have been a real expectation of profit for the butcher. I am not so sure it was for Mr. Danby. However, the problem is there. How do we handle the distinction between business expenses and personal expenses for an artist, especially when that artist is going to go for a long time without making any profit? So again, we invite the Committee to give us some guidelines on that.
There are parallels here again which help the Committee. The Committee might look at the problem of farm losses, how farmers set themselves up and how the tax department treats young farmers or new farm businesses incurring initial losses with the hope of getting a profit. Again we would ask the Committee to bring us the artists' perspective and we will try and turn that into some workable law.
The question of profit helps us with businesses to distinguish between genuine practitioners and phonies. There is a problem we run into with all fields of human endeavour. It is just as true in the arts as it is anywhere else. There are people who are hobbyists, there are people who would love to have the tax write-offs but have not really earned them. They are not really artists, they are hobbyists. The Committee should give us some indication of ways to distinguish between those who are practising a hobby and who want to go to Greece and paint a Grecian sunset. How do we know they are legitimate and should write off the airline tickets and hotel bills and whatever
Income Tax Act
else is incurred, as opposed to some struggling, genuine artists who may be just walking out into the country to paint sunsets there? How do we tell the difference between the two?
Finally, we have the controversy mentioned by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North, the question of employees versus the self-employed. This has real ramifications beyond the arts. We get into problems with engineers, with professionals in other areas, with people who just set up little companies in order to get tax dodges. Again the Committee should give us some indication of how we distinguish between genuine artists who are self-employed and those people who have put themselves in real employee circumstances. That is a tricky area, not one to be treated lightly at all. We should keep our eyes on the ramifications in other areas as well.
I think the motion has presented an important topic and I personally welcome it. I welcome the guidance the Right Hon. Member has given us in his comments and I hope my own comments pass along a few more guidelines for the Committee. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move:
(a)	by deleting line 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"That the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture review all"
That puts the material into the Committee. Further:
(b)	by deleting line 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"taxation of visual and performing artists and writers including, but not"
That includes writers in our consideration. The same happens with my third amendment:
(c)	by deleting line 5 and substituting the following therefor:
"of visual and performing artists and of writers and the method for determin-"
(d)	by adding immediately after line 8 the following:
"That such review be conducted as part of the Committee's study of the Applebaum-Hebert Report and its conclusions on this matter be reported to the House before the Committee continues to other topics within this Report;"
(e)	by deleting line 10 and substituting the following therefor:
"the views of interested parties and organizations."
(/) by deleting lines 11 to 19 inclusive.
Very briefly, those amendments put this motion into the Standing Committee that is equipped to handle it. The motion ensures that the Standing Committee will deal with the matter as a top priority, that it will report back to the House with its findings and that it will include writers as well as visual artists and performing artists.
Finally, there is a chance that the House will prorogue before all of this is done and we will ask our House Leaders to include this item in their negotiations and that the reference be continued on into the next session.

speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, let me pay tribute to the remarks made by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark). This is his first intervention in the House in some time. It seemed to me that he not only chose an area which needs the kind of weight he can bring to a motion, but he did so so eloquently and in such detail that there is very little left for anyone else to say. 1 suggest that not only his eloquence but the wisdom of his remarks is already bearing fruit on the Government side because it has now offered an agreement to send this matter to a committee. I will respond to that agreement on behalf of our Party in a moment.
Since 1 do not want to talk out our own motion, I will underline only three points. First, there was much made of the proposition that this was somehow a new matter that has come upon us and which we must deal with quickly. While we must deal with it quickly, it is certainly not a new matter. This issue has been in existence since 1972, as the Right Hon. Member has said. Indeed, the Disney Report was published in 1978. That report is the basis upon which the Committee can answer many of the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher). Indeed, I suggest that if this report had been dealt with by the Government when it was first published five years ago, we would not have the kind of problem that exists now, where artists are finding it almost impossible to figure how to go about the business of creativity without either going to jail or going broke.
I simply say that the questions being raised were not raised for the first time today by the Hon. Member for Mississauga North. The Disney Report dealt with this problem five years ago. We would have saved people a lot of pain if the Government had dealt with it then.
The second point I want to underline is that we are talking about the importance of establishing a tax status for artists. Again, this is not something new. While it is new to the Government, it is not new, as noted in the Disney Report, to 14 other countries surrounding us. Countries in the western world have been doing this for a decade. Those countries which appreciate the importance of art to them have found a way to deal with the tax status of artists so they can continue to be artists. The important function of the Committee will be to recommend a tax status for artists which will allow them to be artists in this country.
The third point I want to emphasize is something which the right hon. gentleman mentioned earlier. This is not a small matter. Artists are small in number but they are fundamentally important not only to us but our children and our grandchildren. The only way that people in this country know who they are and where they are going is ultimately through performing
artists, writers, sculptors or musicians. We learn who we are and where we are going through art. Surely it is not beyond the competence of this House and the Committee to come up with a status which allows those people who define who we are to be able to do so.
With respect to the agreement offered by the Government, we agree with the motion and that is why I seconded it. We do so with the understanding that the Government has undertaken to raise the matter of prorogation with the House Leaders if, indeed, the matter will die as a consequence of the House being prorogued. Second, we also accept that it is clearly understood that the artists and those affected by the legislation will be heard by the Committee. Third, we accept the proposition that the Government will do its best to bring forward the resources at its command within National Revenue to make sure, at the end of all of this, that we are not simply talking once more but actually doing something for the artists of this country. That will make this day possible.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly welcome this opportunity to speak for a couple of moments about the Right Hon. Member's interest and concern in this question. While it does not fall within the mandate or directly affect the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), it does affect directly the community for which the Minister of Communications is responsible. On that basis we certainly welcome the opportunity to speak to this matter which has come before the House.
As the Hon. Member knows, the question of the methods whereby the federal Government creates a climate in which the arts can flourish has been a matter of intense study by the Government over the past three years. The report of the federal cultural policy review committee has already been mentioned. The Standing Committee on Communications and Culture has, of course, looked at one phase of this, that dealing with broadcasting and film. Certainly it is the intent of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture to review the entire Applebaum-Hebert Report. As a matter of fact, just yesterday the Standing Committee voted to seek a renewal of that reference in any new session so that it might continue the work already begun. Certainly the question of the tax treatment of artists is a priority among the issues that will be examined in that context.
I agree with the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) when he suggests that we should be able to call witnesses to that Committee. Witnesses from all endeavours of the artistic community should be heard so that we can properly understand this very burning problem in which the artistic community is now engaged. We certainly want it rectified.
1 think that has already been proven on this side of the House by the work done by the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. While I recognize the urgency of the Right Hon. Member's motion, 1 too would like to add my voice to the opinion that the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture is the proper forum to study this particular question.
November 2, 1983

It certainly would be irresponsible of me to assure Members that total solutions will be found. As Russell Disney prefaced the recommendations in his famous report, the problems he was dealing with were the residual hard core of issues where fundamental differences of opinion and principle exist between fiscal policy and cultural policy. Mr. Speaker, before addressing the substance of this motion, I would like to point out to Hon. Members that cannabis offences are not presently under the Criminal Code. They are covered under the Narcotic
28652

November 2, 1983
Narcotics
Control Act. The fact that the Hon. Member earlier made this mistake is not untypical of the confusion regarding the current laws on cannabis and the proposals contained in the Speech from the Throne for reform of these laws.
Since the announcement in the Speech from the Throne, the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) and his colleagues, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), have received many letters and phone calls from individuals concerned that the Government intends to legalize cannabis or in fact reduce the status of the offence to that of a traffic violation. They are concerned that the Government is condoning the use of a potentially noxious substance. Let me state categorically that this is not and was never the intention of the Government, and surely it was no intention of mine as a Private Member. As was stated by the Minister of Justice in an appearance before the Justice and Legal Affairs Committee of the House of Commons on May 26, 1981, concerning cannabis, he said:
It is our intention to bring about changes which will serve to lessen the severity of the penalties for possession of this substance, without ''legalizing" or even "decriminalizing" marijuana. The Government believes that marijuana is a health hazard and intends to launch an active public education program among Canadians, especially the younger members of our society, to continue to discourage its use. Furthermore, we will continue to prosecute with vigor all those who traffic in this drug.
This statement is self-evident and is a direct quotation.
The Government does not condone the use of marijuana and other cannabis products by Canadians. That should be clearly understood by all Members of the House as well as the general public. We are concerned with the adverse health and safety effects of drug use and will be doing more to inform Canadians in this area.
As a high school teacher some years ago we found in many of the schools in our area cannabis was beginning to be a problem. I am happy to say from the information forthcoming in the last few years this problem has subsided somewhat. This is an encouraging sign for those still in education and for myself in public life who must deal with these problems on a weekly basis.
Why did the Government propose to change the cannabis laws? The pressure for change stems from the inadequacies and unfortunate consequences of the application of the present law. Under the current legislation, possession of cannabis, even in minimal quantity, exposes a person to the possibility of damaging criminal records entailing difficulties in terms of social stigma, employment and immigration. In the past ten years more than 200,000 Canadians have been found guilty of possession of cannabis, and in spite of considerable enforcement efforts, an increasing number of Canadians use cannabis, indicating an apparent lack of effectiveness of the law. The cost to society of using the full weight of the criminal process to discourage cannabis use has been very high, and I might add with very little return.
During the course of the next few minutes, I would like to indicate some of the background factors which influenced the
Government to initiate its study on the problems of cannabis use and cannabis laws per se. Cannabis is not an opiate narcotic in any pharmacological sense, yet the control of cannabis is now under the Narcotic Control Act along with such other substances as heroin and cocaine. This may be due to the fact that little was known about cannabis back in 1923 when it was first added to the schedule of prohibited narcotics under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act of 1920.
It is unfortunate that cannabis has been grouped together with narcotics because in the public mind they are seen to be equally harmful substances with the same addictive properties, producing the same physiological damage. The Narcotic Control Act is reserved for more harmful drugs, the narcotics. Therefore, the law regulating the control of these substances is much more severe. This fact is worth nothing because 1 think the general public is unaware of the penalties listed in the law when they hear or read about courts giving discharges to offenders. The Food and Drugs Act is the statute reserved for the control of non-narcotic drugs that may be subject to abuse. Many argue that cannabis more properly belongs under that statute. I want to make clear at this point that this is not my view. I am not convinced as a Private Member that it should come under the Food and Drugs Act.
It may come as a surprise to Hon. Members to learn that the maximum penalty in law for possession of cannabis is seven years, if it is proceeded with as an indictable offence. Normally it is proceeded with as a summary conviction offence, in which case the maximum penalty is $1,000 and/or six months for a first offence and $2,000 and/or one year for a subsequent offence. The offences of trafficking and importing carry very severe penalties, up to life imprisonment. In the case of importing, it is further specified that the minimum sentence is to be seven years imprisonment, with a maximum of life imprisonment also. I state categorically that for those people trafficking in drugs and importing them, I believe the full force of the law should be applied.
Unauthorized or simple possession of cannabis is the offence which concerns us most. I believe it is what we are discussing today. It is the most frequent offence and the one that results in so many of our young people being perceived as criminals. Simple possession is a hybrid offence, that is to say, punishable either on summary conviction or by way of indictment. However, at the initial stage it is treated as an indictable offence, which means that the individual is usually fingerprinted and photographed and a centralized permanent police record is created. Hundreds of thousands of Canadians, many of whom would not have otherwise become involved in this stigmatizing process, have been fingerprinted and photographed for simple possession of cannabis; some have even been imprisoned. In addition, the majority of those charged are found guilty and now bear the burden of a damaging record.
The fact that many people are breaking the law and being convicted is not reason enough to change it. However the law should reflect the gravity of the conduct penalized. The current high maximums relating to simple possession of cannabis products bear no relationship to present sentencing practices
November 2, 1983

and can hardly be justified with respect to any offence of a basically non-violent nature where the main victim is the user. Here again I digress. If we were to take this statement as it is, there would be the implication that we would be condoning the use of cannabis. That is our last idea. Because it is so damaging to the people who use it-and it is my belief that the Le Dain Commission which brought down its report some years ago did not have the facts at its disposal which we now have-we must make decisions on behalf of Canadians.
The law should also reflect the attitudes of Canadians generally. In this regard it is worth noting that national surveys conducted in 1977 and 1978 indicated that about two-thirds of the population was in favour of either a regulatory scheme or minor penalties for possession of cannabis. Only one-third favoured the present law or something more severe. 1 count myself among that third. A survey conducted in 1980 confirmed that this support has remained about the same, with some increase in favour of the status quo.
A Gallup omnibus study on marijuana, jointly commissioned by the Department of Justice, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Ministry of the Solicitor General in August and September, 1981, explored a different aspect of marijuana control-the severity of penalties imposed by the courts. In terms of the perceived appropriateness of the sentences imposed by the courts for possession of marijuana, 15 per cent of the respondents thought the penalties were too heavy, 26 per cent thought they were about right, and 36 per cent thought they were too light. The remainder, 23 per cent, had no opinion or thought that possession was legal. A clear majority of respondents believed that penalties imposed by the courts for trafficking and importing marijuana were too light. The point which has to be emphasized in the House of Commons is that when we are dealing with trafficking and importing, these are the people who must be stamped out; they must be caught and must be the ones who are most severely punished by society.
Hear, hear!

Also the survey indicated that over 80 per cent of respondents said that a change in the law would not affect their decisions concerning whether or not to use marijuana and, in the case of users, how often to use it. About one in six
Narcotics
respondents reported knowing of someone who had been caught by the police for possession of marijuana. In virtually all these cases, those apprehended were reported to have experienced problems, namely with their families and arising from having a criminal record.
The reform of cannabis legislation has been commented upon by a variety of interest groups. Some of these, such as NORML-the National Organization for the Reform of Marijuana Laws-have been organized specifically for this purpose. Most others, such as the Canadian Medical Association and the Canadian Bar Association, have commented upon it due to the interest of their members.
From the public pronouncements of these various groups there does emerge a consensus. Generally they agree that possession of cannabis should remain an offence, with which I agree; that it should be shifted to the Food and Drugs Act, about which I have reservations; that the consequences of conviction should be reduced. If they mean the consequences of conviction with regard to those people who are caught, I do not know that 1 would want to go that way. The consequences of conviction also imply that we are dealing with the families of people who are known or caught using this narcotic. Finally, they agreed unanimously that there should be increased efforts at public education, with which I believe everyone in the House would agree.
Reform of cannabis laws is not a recent issue. This matter was considered previously by the Government. As a result of the Le Dain Commission which was completed in 1973, there were several tentative steps toward reform. The House may recall that the Government introduced Bill S-19 in the Senate. The Senate passed that Bill but it died on the House of Commons Order Paper at the end of the 1974-75 session of the Thirtieth Parliament. The problems associated with the current law continue, so this most recent initiative to review the law was launched by the Government.
